This document provides detailed recommendations for hand hygiene practices to be followed by healthcare workers caring for patients with filovirus infections, such as Ebola and Marburg viruses. These recommendations were developed using WHO's Rapid Advice Guideline procedures and are based on systematic reviews of scientific evidence and expert consensus. Recommendation 1: WHO strongly recommends performing hand hygiene using either an alcohol-based hand rub or soap and running water, following the correct technique as outlined by WHO. Alcohol-based hand rubs should be available at every point of care, including at the entrance and within isolation rooms, as they are considered the standard of care. If alcohol-based hand rubs are unavailable, hand hygiene should be performed with soap and running water whenever necessary. When hands are visibly soiled, hand hygiene must always be performed with soap and running water. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of alcohol-based hand rubs and soap and water in eliminating microorganisms, including viruses. The preferred use of alcohol-based hand rubs is based on several factors: Their ability to eliminate the majority of microorganisms, including viruses. The short time required for microbicidal activity (20–30 seconds). Their availability at the point of care. Better skin tolerance compared to other methods. No need for specific infrastructure, such as clean water supply, washbasins, soap, or hand towels. Handwashing with soap and water is also highly effective at removing microbial contamination, although specific data for filoviruses are lacking. Expert consensus suggests that handwashing with soap and water is effective against enveloped viruses. Proper technique and duration are crucial for achieving the desired effect, whether using alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and water. For alcohol-based hand rubs, WHO recommends applying a palmful of the product to cover all hand surfaces and rubbing for 20–30 seconds until dry. For handwashing, hands should be wet with clean, running water, and a sufficient amount of soap should be applied to cover all surfaces. Hands should then be rinsed with water and dried thoroughly with a single-use towel. The entire procedure should last 40–60 seconds. Recommendation 2: In settings where bleach or chlorine solutions are currently used for hand hygiene, WHO strongly recommends transitioning to alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and water. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence for the effectiveness of alcohol-based hand rubs and soap and water. WHO emphasizes the importance of providing access to a safe, continuous water supply and the necessary facilities for handwashing, as well as ensuring the availability of alcohol-based hand rubs at the point of patient care. National governments are urged to prioritize improved hand hygiene adherence and consider implementing funded, coordinated programs with monitoring and long-term sustainability. Recommendation 3: Bleach or chlorine solutions currently used for hand hygiene and glove disinfection may be used temporarily in emergency situations until alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and water become available. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence regarding the comparative efficacy of bleach/chlorine solutions versus alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and water. Limited evidence suggests that 0.05% chlorine solution can be effective against filoviruses when used for hand hygiene, provided it is applied for 40–60 seconds until hands are dry. However, there is very limited evidence on the potential skin irritation or lesions caused by bleach/chlorine solutions. While low concentrations of bleach/chlorine solutions do not appear to cause respiratory irritation or asthma, respiratory symptoms have been reported in individuals exposed to these solutions during environmental decontamination. There is also evidence of a risk of irritative conjunctivitis from exposure to bleach/chlorine solutions. From a dermatological perspective, alcohol-based hand rubs are considered the best option for hand hygiene due to their superior skin tolerance and lower risk of skin barrier impairment. Safety measures and assessments are essential in settings where bleach/chlorine solutions are used for hand hygiene. While bleach/chlorine solutions may be acceptable when other agents are unavailable, alcohol-based hand rubs are generally preferred. Glove Disinfection: In the context of Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreaks, glove disinfection has been considered to reduce the need for frequent glove changes, which carry a high risk of healthcare worker hand contamination. A two-step procedure is recommended: disinfecting the outer gloves before removing them safely and disinfecting the inner gloves before donning a fresh outer pair. Alcohol-based hand rubs are preferred for disinfecting gloved hands, but bleach/chlorine solutions are acceptable if alcohol-based products are unavailable. Background: Filovirus infections, such as Ebola and Marburg viruses, are among the most severe and feared viral hemorrhagic fevers, with high case fatality rates. Most outbreaks occur after zoonotic infections, followed by person-to-person transmission, often in settings with inadequate infection prevention and control measures. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected body fluids or contaminated surfaces, with no documented transmission through intact skin. Hand hygiene best practices and appropriate glove use are essential to protect healthcare workers and prevent transmission to others. However, no single infection control measure is effective on its own; a comprehensive package of measures, including administrative, environmental, and engineering controls, is necessary. The WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care, issued in 2009, recommend alcohol-based hand rubs as the preferred method for routine hand antisepsis in clinical settings unless hands are visibly soiled, in which case handwashing with soap and water is required. These guidelines are based on systematic evidence reviews, expert consensus, and pilot testing and are considered the gold standard for hand hygiene practices. However, in African countries affected by the EVD outbreak, chlorine solutions are widely used due to limited availability of alcohol-based hand rubs and soap, ease of use, and fear-driven reliance on environmental disinfectants.
